Image location: Switzerland
First I thought this might be southern Germany because of the straight-clipped hedges and dense deciduous woodland lining the road.
But that cannot be, because German license plates always feature a blue EU strip on the left side whereas this van plate lacks it; road shoulders use red-painted asphalt strips which are distinctly Swiss for deceleration zones; and the yield sign pole has a minimalist design without the typical German reflector bands.
Another possibility was Austria due to the similar tidy rural landscape and central European trees.
However, Austrian plates use a blue-white color scheme or different formatting unlike this plain white Swiss-style plate; no "S" cantonal code or eagle emblem visible as in AT; and the road lacks Austrian-specific white rumble strips on edges.
The correct clues are: red asphalt on road shoulders and apron for safety deceleration typical of Swiss roads; white reflective license plate with black letters in Swiss format lacking EU blue band; yield sign (red circle with white inverted triangle) on slim pole standard in CH; small route marker near signpost indicating cantonal road numbering like "46"; tall uniform privet hedges common in Swiss suburbs; mix of chestnut and maple trees with late-summer foliage matching Bernese lowlands.
This photo was taken in Switzerland.
Latitude: 46.9594°N, Longitude: 7.755°E

<image>
Think step by step...

Image location: Dominican Republic
First I thought this might be Puerto Rico because of the dense royal palms, white stucco buildings with barred gates, and tropical residential vibe common in San Juan suburbs.
But that cannot be, because no US-style license plates or bilingual signs, road markings lack PR's bold white stop lines, power poles have DR's typical clustered transformers, and the stone masonry bases on houses are chunkier than PR's smoother concrete.
Another possibility was coastal Colombia due to the modern gated compounds, overhanging power lines, and palm-lined streets seen in Cartagena outskirts.
However, vegetation shows Caribbean royal palms (Roystonea) not Colombia's wax palms, cars are right-hand drive imports like Toyota Corollas common in DR not left-hand Colombian models, no Spanish graffiti or tropical ferns, and paving uses reddish clay bricks absent in Colombian asphalt norms.
The correct clues are: royal palms (Roystonea oleracea) lining walls, beige stone-and-plaster house architecture with flat roofs and metal grilles, reddish brick-paved sidewalks with grass strips, white sedans matching DR's imported Hyundai/Toyota fleet, tangled overhead wires on wooden poles with DR-style insulators, yellow pedestrian crossing arrow markings.
This photo was taken in Dominican Republic.
Latitude: 18.515°N, Longitude: 70.4368°W

Image location: Albania
First I thought this might be Greece because of the olive trees and dry Mediterranean scrub vegetation.
But that cannot be, because the power poles use simple wooden crossarms without the concrete bases common in Greece; the road arrows are basic white chevrons painted directly on dirt unlike Greek reflective standards; the building has a utilitarian metal roof without typical Greek tile detailing.
Another possibility was southern Italy due to the rural dirt road and sparse hillside scrub.
However, Italian rural areas rarely have such prominent olive groves mixed with acacia bushes at this elevation; power lines lack the multi-wire bundling seen in Italy; no vine trellises or stone walls typical of Italian countryside.
The correct clues are: distinctive olive trees with silvery leaves common in Albanian hillsides; simple whitewashed building with sloped corrugated metal roof typical of rural Albanian farm sheds; dirt road with crudely painted white directional arrows standard on unpaved Albanian backroads; wooden utility poles with basic H-frame crossarms prevalent in Balkan infrastructure; hilly terrain with dry grass and scattered bushes matching Albanian interior landscapes; cloudy overcast sky frequent in Albanian mountain valleys.

First I thought this might be Peru because the Andean mountains in the background and central plaza with porticoed buildings resemble highland towns like Cusco outskirts.
But that cannot be, because Peruvian plazas often feature more adobe-style construction without the vibrant red roofs; palm trees are rarer in Peruvian highlands at this elevation; road markings use yellow centers more frequently, not these white directional arrows; latitude would be further south around 12°S.
Another possibility was Ecuador due to the equatorial latitude range, tropical palms mixed with steep green mountains, and Spanish colonial square layout.
However, Ecuadorian Street View shows more frequent "Transito" signs and volcanic warnings absent here; building facades lack Ecuador's typical pastel greens and have bolder reds/blues; license plate styles (if glimpsed nearby) use yellow backgrounds unlike Colombia's white; power poles have distinct ceramic insulators not matching.
The correct clues are: vibrant red-tiled roofs and blue/white facades on two-story buildings with verandas; clusters of queen palms (Washingtonia robusta) framing the plaza typical of Colombian inter-Andean valleys; geometric red-paver plaza stones with central seating areas; tall cylindrical lamp posts with pointed tops standard in Cundinamarca region; steep, lush cloud-forest-covered mountains under frequent overcast skies; white road arrows and curbside markings matching Colombian highway standards.
This photo was taken in Colombia.

Image location: Finland
First I thought this might be Sweden because of the falun red and white wooden houses with brown roofs and surrounding birch trees.
But that cannot be, because Swedish rural houses often feature more curved gables and tile roofs; utility poles lack the straight double-crossarm design typical of Finland; no yellow center line on the gravel road as in Sweden; birch undergrowth is sparser with more mossy rocks there.
Another possibility was Norway due to the remote rural scenery, gravel driveway, and northern birch vegetation.
However, Norwegian countryside shows steeper terrain and chalet-style roofs with overhangs; houses have darker wood staining over paint; fewer straight birches and more spruce dominance; no cable TV boxes mounted low on poles like in Finland.
The correct clues are: Finnish-style electricity poles with horizontal double crossarms and insulators; classic red-painted barn/garage with white trim and flat roof; dense stand of slender white-barked birches with grassy understory; curved private gravel driveway typical of Finnish summer cottages; wooden outbuilding resembling a sauna annex; subtle northern summer light with fresh green foliage at high latitude.

Image location: Cambodia
First I thought this might be Thailand because of the dense scooter traffic, tropical roadside vegetation like palms, and colorful shopfronts with awnings.
But that cannot be, because the signs use distinctly rounded Khmer script instead of Thai's curved script; license plates are white with a blue upper stripe and Khmer numerals unlike Thailand's black-and-yellow plates; and the tuk-tuks are moto-pulled trailers typical of Cambodia, not Thailand's auto-rickshaws.
Another possibility was Vietnam due to the bustling urban street with two-story shophouses, street vendors, and humid tropical skyline.
However, Vietnamese signage would feature Latin script with diacritics rather than pure Khmer script here; vehicle plates show Cambodia's rectangular format with the Angkor Wat emblem area, not Vietnam's blue-on-white provincial codes; and the architecture has more pronounced French-colonial stucco balconies without Vietnam's typical ceramic roof tiles.
The correct clues are: Khmer-language signs on pharmacies and shops (e.g., green-cross pharmacy with "ឱសថ" script); Cambodian license plates (white fields, blue header with kingdom coat-of-arms); moto-remorque tuk-tuks parked prominently; French-era two-story buildings with wrought-iron balconies and pastel facades; roadside utility poles with Khmer warning labels; and dry-season scrubby palms mixed with rice paddy hints in the background.
This photo was taken in Cambodia.
Latitude: 12.2886°N, Longitude: 104.9954°E

Image location: Costa Rica
First I thought this might be Mexico because of the colonial-era church interior with religious paintings and statues typical of Latin American Catholicism.
But that cannot be, because Mexican churches rarely feature such vibrant turquoise-green arabesque wall tiles; the floor shows distinctive yellow-starred geometric patterns not common in Mexican religious sites; the statue's blue gown and pedestal style lacks the ornate shelving seen in Mexican interiors.
Another possibility was Portugal due to the intricate patterned wall tiles evoking azulejo designs.
However, Portuguese azulejos are predominantly blue-and-white rather than green; no maritime or historical motifs typical of Iberian churches; the parquet-style floor with bold black-white checks and Moorish stars is more New World colonial; the dim lighting and tropical humidity cues in the paint aging don't match European climates.
The correct clues are: turquoise-green walls covered in white arabesque and geometric tiles unique to Costa Rican church renovations; black-white-yellow checkered floor with embedded star motifs echoing Spanish Moorish influence localized in Central America; large framed paintings of reclining saints in white robes suggestive of Costa Rican devotional art; blue-robed female statue on a wooden shelf typical of Costa Rican Marian iconography; arched corners and fresco borders matching interiors like those in Pérez Zeledón region churches; subtle tropical wood grain in the floor and frames indicating humid neotropical environment.
This photo was taken in Costa Rica.
Latitude: 9.2765°N, Longitude: 84.0512°W

Image location: Mongolia
First I thought this might be Kyrgyzstan because of the rugged, hilly terrain and scattered rural housing with simple construction.
But that cannot be, because the vegetation is extremely sparse with dry brown grass instead of greener alpine meadows; the houses have unusually vibrant pink and red sheet-metal roofs uncommon in Kyrgyz villages; power poles are simple wooden with overhead wires in a distinctly sparse Mongolian grid pattern; and the road is unpaved gravel without the typical Kyrgyz concrete barriers or stone walls.
Another possibility was rural Kazakhstan due to the arid steppe-like landscape and wooden fences.
However, the fences here are tall palisade-style with sharply pointed tops specific to Mongolian suburbs; house walls are beige plaster over block with no Kazakh whitewashed adobe; hills are rocky and barren without Kazakh black soil patches; and the valley settlement layout matches Mongolian ger-district outskirts, not Kazakh auls.
The correct clues are: vibrant pink/red sheet-metal roofs on squat houses typical of peri-urban Mongolia; tall wooden palisade fences with V-shaped points ubiquitous in Mongolian settlements; barren rocky hills with zero trees and dry tan grass indicating cold steppe climate; simple overhead power lines on tapered wooden poles standard in Mongolia; gravel road with subtle wheel ruts and no markings common in rural Mongolian valleys; south-facing aspect revealing distant ger-like structures on hillsides.
This photo was taken in Mongolia.

Image location: Nigeria
First I thought this might be Ghana because of the corrugated metal roofs, concrete block buildings, and dusty unpaved roads common in West African suburbs.
But that cannot be, because the buildings feature prominent red iron reinforcement frames protruding upward for future floors, a distinctly Nigerian construction practice; the utility poles are tall wooden types with simple cross-arms and tangled overhead wires unlike Ghana's often concrete poles; the sparse yellowish savanna grass and open terrain differ from Ghana's lusher tropical edges; white directional arrows painted directly on the dirt road are a Nigerian rural marking style.
Another possibility was rural India due to the dusty track, simple block architecture, and overhead power lines.
However, exposed rebar skeletons on half-built structures are rare in Indian villages; vegetation lacks India's typical dense scrub or palms, showing dry African grass instead; road has bold white chevron arrows not seen in Indian dirt paths; building walls use pinkish plaster over blocks unlike India's brickier style.
The correct clues are: protruding red steel reinforcement bars on upper building levels for ongoing expansion; white painted arrows and chevrons marking the dirt road; tall wooden electricity poles with multiple cross-arms and dense wire clusters; corrugated galvanized roofs with rust patches on low-rise homes; unfinished concrete block walls in earth tones and pink; sparse dry savanna grass patches amid urban sprawl.
This photo was taken in Nigeria.
Latitude: 8.8004°N, Longitude: 8.7693°E

But that cannot be, because the road has a solid white edge line on the driver's right side with dashed center markings specific to German highways; the embankment drainage ditches are wider and grass-lined unlike Polish styles; no bilingual signs or typical Eastern European utility poles; and the pines are more uniform Scots pine without Polish birch understory.
Another possibility was Sweden due to the coniferous woodland and clear northern skies.
However, Swedish roads feature reflective yellow edge lines and wider shoulders; no snow berms or gravel verges; utility wires are underground or on concrete poles not wooden; and the terrain lacks Swedish rocky outcrops.
The correct clues are: solid white road edge line and dashed center line standard on German B-roads; Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) monoculture with low deciduous shrubs matching central German forestry; sandy soil with dry grass and heather-like scrub indicating Hessian lowlands; steep roadside embankment with anti-erosion matting typical of German Autobahn-adjacent paths; smooth asphalt surface without Swedish-style chipseal patches; north German Street View coverage angle and pegman style.

First I thought this might be Greece because of the sunny outdoor cafe with red umbrellas and beige awning evoking a Mediterranean taverna vibe.
But that cannot be, because the license plates are black with white letters and "AL" code unlike Greek blue-white EU plates, Latin alphabet on signs instead of Greek script, and the tall brutalist apartment block differs from whitewashed Greek architecture.
Another possibility was Montenegro due to the similar compact European cars like the blue Fiat and Fiat-like silver sedan parked curbside in a hilly area.
However, Montenegrin plates are white with red/black lettering and "MNE" code, no Montenegrin Cyrillic signage visible, road edges and vegetation lean more Albanian highland scrub than Adriatic coast, and balcony styles on the building are distinctly Albanian communist-era.

Another possibility was Colombia due to the similar humid tropical greenery and scattered rural buildings with metal roofs.
However, the vehicle's plate shows Brazilian state coding (likely MT for Mato Grosso), architecture features whitewashed block walls atypical for Andean Colombia, no Spanish signage visible, and drier soil exposure rules out the wetter Llanos region.
The correct clues are: Brazilian license plate with white background and black lettering in MERCOSUL style, cerrado vegetation with scattered palms and acacia-like trees, simple cinderblock houses with red clay tile roofs, dirt road with gravel shoulders typical of interior Brazil, wooden utility poles with transformer boxes, and overall savanna landscape matching Mato Grosso.

But that cannot be, because vehicles display white plates with blue "SK" EU strips instead of "HU"; street signs and route markers use standard Slovak formatting without Hungarian bilingual elements; the license plate fonts and layout precisely match Slovak standards; hilly Carpathian terrain lacks the Pannonian plain feel.
Another possibility was Poland due to the similar Eastern European rural road scene with white license plates, vans, and zebra crossings.

The correct clues are: white license plates with blue "SK" country code on multiple cars including the red sedan and white van; yellow road sign indicating Slovak route 51 towards the Orava region; distinctive railway station building with red mansard roof, white stucco facade, and green shutters typical of northern Slovak ZSSK stations; Carpathian foothills with mixed deciduous-coniferous vegetation and distant industrial chimney; European road markings with white dashed lines, red-white bollards, and concrete barriers standard in Slovakia; street lamps with single arm and rectangular base common in Slovak towns.
This photo was taken in Slovakia.

But that cannot be, because there are no stone walls or ivy-covered buildings typical of the Northeast, the attached two-car garages look more modern Plains-style rather than historic Colonial, the boxy hedges and sparse trees indicate a drier prairie climate, and the double yellow center lines with prominent fog lines are more common west of the Appalachians.

However, the lack of tall evergreens or mossy vegetation rules that out, the houses use vinyl siding instead of the Pacific Northwest's wood shakes or brick, utility poles have Southwestern crossarm styles without coastal hardware, and the parking booth architecture matches Midwest complexes not rainy urban areas.

"PARKING" labeled booth at a multi-unit garage entrance typical of Oklahoma apartment lots, 2. beige/gray vinyl siding and asphalt shingle roofs on suburban homes common in Tulsa-area developments, 3. manicured box hedges and low prairie grasses showing semi-arid Plains vegetation, 4. wooden utility poles with multiple crossarms and transformers standard in rural Oklahoma, 5. double solid yellow center line with white dashed edges and yellow fog line matching Oklahoma DOT road standards, 6. blurred license plates in the rectangular US Great Plains shape without coastal or Eastern designs.

But that cannot be, because the license plate on the black sedan follows Portugal's format with a central dash and no Spanish provincial codes; the guardrails use white-capped metal posts uncommon in southern Spain; road arrows are purely white without yellow centers typical in Spain; and the lamp post has a slender Iberian design not matching Andalusian styles.

However, the right-hand drive with European plate design eliminates the US; no yellow center lines or rumble strips visible; guardrails lack American W-beam style; and the Street View UI overlays match Google Earth formats used in Europe.
The correct clues are: Portuguese license plate (white background, black alpha-numeric with vertical dash separator); metal guardrails on concrete Jersey barriers with white posts standard on Portuguese A-roads; white lane-merge arrows and dashed edge lines per Portuguese highway code; dry grassland and olive-like scrub vegetation of central Portugal; tall, straight lamp posts with single arm typical of IPMA regions; reservoir shoreline matching the Tagus River valley near Santarém.

Another possibility was Belarus due to the rural riverine landscape and coniferous forest edges.
However, no Cyrillic signage or markings visible, more advanced concrete-and-steel bridge construction without Soviet-era rust, brighter green grass indicating wetter temperate climate, and lack of typical Belarusian birch dominance.
The correct clues are: galvanized metal pedestrian bridge with horizontal bar railings and mesh infill common on Polish rural paths, mixed pine and deciduous trees (poplars, willows) lining the riverbanks, lush grassy meadows with wildflowers typical of central Polish lowlands, calm slow-flowing river with muddy banks and reed edges, overcast gray skies frequent in Mazovia region, flat terrain with subtle glacial moraine undulations.

However, panelák color schemes here match Czech preferences (peach/orange with green accents over beige); latitude places it north of typical Slovak sites; no Slovak bilingual signs or plates; and the crosswalk arrow markings follow Czech norms without Slovak deviations.
The correct clues are: Czech street name "Na Hradbě" on map overlay; classic 10-story paneláks with slanted roofs and facade stripes unique to Czechia; prohibited road marking with bold red X typical of Czech highways; slim cylindrical street lamps with single arms standard in Czech suburbs; small utilitarian booth with red door and sloped roof like Czech transformer stations; central European early-spring bushes and bare deciduous trees.

Image location: Tunisia
First I thought this might be southern Spain (Andalusia) because of the whitewashed perimeter walls and Mediterranean-style oleander hedges.
But that cannot be, because the walls are unusually high and featureless without typical Spanish tile coping or decorative gates; the road markings are minimalistic with a thin white directional arrow unlike Europe's standardized thicker lines; utility poles use simple concrete posts with overhead wire bundles atypical for EU infrastructure; and the vegetation shows salt-tolerant shrubs thriving in sandier soil.
Another possibility was southern California, USA due to the suburban street layout, stucco-like white walls, and irrigated greenery under clear blue skies.
However, the absence of curbside fire hydrants or mailboxes rules that out; sidewalks are narrow and uneven without poured concrete perfection; no overhead power lines in the American style but rather rural crossarms; and the bushes have a denser, thorny North African profile rather than manicured succulents.
The correct clues are: high windowless white concrete walls enclosing properties, a hallmark of private residential security in Tunisian suburbs; vibrant green oleander hedges with subtle reddish tinges lining the walls; tall, feathery-topped acacia trees providing sparse shade; basic asphalt road with a single white chevron arrow indicating right-hand traffic flow; slender concrete utility pole with multi-wire distribution typical of Maghrebi grids; arid backdrop with irrigated pockets suggesting coastal Sahel region agriculture.
This photo was taken in Tunisia.

However, British road markings including the white chevron yield markings at the junction, left-hand traffic flow with vehicles parked on the left, Leylandii conifer trees in gardens atypical for France, and no metric speed signs or French plates rule that out.
The correct clues are: pebble-dashed bungalows with dormer windows and brick extensions typical of Scottish lowlands suburbs, tall Leyland cypress hedges and evergreen shrubs in domestic gardens, dry stone walls bounding properties common in central Scotland, UK road markings with broken white center line and edge lines plus yield triangle at bend, overhead phone wires on H-poles with insulators, white uPVC sash-style windows on stone cottages.

But that cannot be, because the arches are rough-hewn stone ruins more typical of North African medinas, the vegetation is sparse Saharan scrub rather than olive groves or maquis, power poles lack the typical Greek ceramic insulators, and cars appear right-hand drive with African truck styles.
Another possibility was southern Spain due to the Moorish-influenced architecture and dry dusty streets.
However, the flat-roofed white buildings lack Spanish tiled accents, no Iberian vegetation like agave or palms in that density, license plate holders on cars suggest regional Arab designs, and the overall urban decay fits Tunisian coastal towns better.
